summary: Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors (MKIDs) with a 1024-pixel array at 150 µm pixel pitch suffer from significant frequency scatter caused by both fabrication variations and tight packing, limiting detector yield for frequency-division multiplexing. Post-fabrication electron-beam trimming of interdigitated capacitor finger lengths reduces frequency scatter from $1.1 	imes 10^{-2}$ to $3.5 	imes 10^{-4}$ and increases yield from 76% to 94% with no degradation in quality factor or noise.
motivation: High multiplexing factors in MKID arrays are limited by resonator frequency collisions arising from fabrication-induced variations and electromagnetic effects of dense pixel layouts. Existing post-fabrication correction methods (laser scanning, contact lithography) lack the spatial resolution needed for tightly packed visible/near-infrared MKID arrays.
method: Electron-beam lithography was used to sequentially trim IDC finger lengths after measuring resonance frequencies via optical row-by-column scanning with a smartphone-based pixel-to-frequency mapper. New target frequencies $F_D^{trim}$ with constant spacing $\lambda_D^{trim}$ were determined from measured frequencies $F_M$, and required trim lengths $l_C^{trim}$ were obtained by fitting the $l_C(F_M)$ relationship with a 6-degree polynomial and interpolating at $F_D^{trim}$.
result: For device A with 1024 pixels and $\lambda_{min} = 8.0 \times 10^{-5}$, yield improved from 76% to 94%; frequency scatter decreased by factor 30. Device comparison (B: 150 µm vs. C: 450 µm pitch) showed spatial patterns increase $\sigma$ by factor 4 at tight pitch, establishing the necessity of trimming for dense arrays. Lower limit of trimming method estimated at $\sigma_\mathrm{lim}^\mathrm{trim} \approx 4.9 \times 10^{-5}$, enabling multiplexing factors near 4000 per octave.
